content.title: NASA and SpaceX vault Crew Dragon with four astronauts on historic mission to ISS
content.text: Updated Nov. 15, 2020, 9:37 p.m. ETRoutine, operational missions to the International Space Station – complete with astronauts – are officially underway.Four astronauts vaulted off Kennedy Space Center's pad 39A at 7:27 p.m. Sunday, kicking off a 27-hour flight in their Crew Dragon capsule and setting the stage for NASA and SpaceX's first full-duration ISS mission. NASA's Victor Glover, Mike Hopkins, and Shannon Walker, along with Japanese astronaut Soichi Noguchi, are slated to dock at 11 p.m. Monday.Under the pressures of the coronavirus pandemic and tumultuous election season, the Crew-1 mission astronauts chose an apt name for their capsule: Resilience."To all the people at NASA and SpaceX: by working together through these difficult times, you've inspired the nation and the world," mission commander Hopkins said just before the Falcon 9 rocket's liftoff. "Now it's time for us to do our part. Crew-1 for all."After launch, the astronauts' 27-foot capsule entered a stable orbit, separated from the second stage, and began its trek to the ISS circling some 250 miles above Earth. "It was a great liftoff," SpaceX engineer John Insprucker said during the company's webcast. "Everything is happening right per the procedure. We've got crew successfully on orbit."The 162-foot booster used for Sunday's flight also successfully landed on the Just Read the Instructions drone ship about nine minutes after liftoff. If hardware checkouts look good, NASA and SpaceX have agreed to re-fly the booster on the next mission known as Crew-2 sometime in the first half of next year.Because Crew Dragon will fly autonomously, pilot Glover won't need to interact with spacecraft controls unless necessary. Even the docking process is entirely automated."Congratulations to NASA and SpaceX on today's launch," President-elect Joe Biden said via Twitter. "It’s a testament to the power of science and what we can accomplish by harnessing our innovation, ingenuity, and determination. I join all Americans and the people of Japan in wishing the astronauts Godspeed on their journey."Once docked and on board, the four astronauts will have packed schedules: station maintenance, conducting science experiments, and vigorous exercise, to name a few. They will join NASA astronaut Kate Rubins and Russian cosmonauts Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergey Ryzhikov.Hopkins is an Air Force colonel and flight test engineer who previously launched to the ISS on a Russian Soyuz rocket. A commander in the Navy, Glover is a test pilot and Crew-1 marks his first flight to space. Walker, a veteran astronaut and physicist, shares the role of mission specialist with Noguchi, who is an aeronautical engineer for the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency.Sunday's launch marks Noguchi's third spaceflight – to date, he has flown on the space shuttle, Soyuz, and now Crew Dragon. Crew-1 is also the first time an American-made capsule has flown with more than three crew members.The crew will spend about six months on the ISS. The effort is part of NASA's Commercial Crew Program, established after the end of the space shuttle to return American astronauts to orbit and end reliance on Russia's Soyuz spacecraft."The big milestone here is that we are now moving away from development and testing and into operational flights," NASA Administrator Jim Bridenstine told reporters after liftoff. "This operational flight was licensed by the FAA, so this is truly a commercial launch."Crew-1 comes after Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley became the first astronauts to fly Crew Dragon for SpaceX's last demonstration mission known as Demo-2. Their capsule successfully launched on May 30, docked, spent about two months on station, then splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico.SpaceX hopes to fly at least two more fully crewed missions for NASA next year. The program also includes Boeing and its Starliner capsule, though its test flight in December 2019 failed to reach orbit due to software issues. The company is expected to conduct its second Starliner test flight – a makeup of the first – sometime after January.Sunday's launch marked the 26th of 2020 for the Space Coast, which could hit 30 before the end of the year. NASA Deputy Administrator Jim Morhard said the area could see as many as 56 launches in 2021."On behalf of SpaceX, thanks for flying Falcon and Dragon and safe travels," Hans Koenigsmann, a vice president at SpaceX, told the crew about an hour after liftoff."Well done, that was one heck of a ride. There were a lot of smiles," Hopkins responded. "Making history is hard and you all made it look easy."Contact Emre Kelly at aekelly@floridatoday.com or 321-242-3715.
